g.text: Reverse-engineering a 3-layer bidirectional transformer that classifies whether a bracket string is balanced. I discover the 'elevation circuit':
head 0.0 tallies opens vs closes over the suffix, MLPs 0/1 threshold it nonlinearly, head 2.0 copies the result from position 1 to position 0.
Math intuition marked ∂ (blue). Prereq / concept boxes marked ★ (yellow). Code cards use mono font. All notes written first-person.
The task + the elevation circuit at a glance
The model classifies strings like '(()())' as balanced or unbalanced. It learned an unusual right-to-left algorithm: compute (closes - opens) over the SUFFIX at each position.
Sequence is unbalanced iff elevation[0] != 0 OR any(elevation < 0). The exercises reverse-engineer WHICH heads implement this.
'(' contributes -1 ')' contributes +1 over the SUFFIX from i to end
Then: unbalanced iff elevation[0] != 0 OR any(elevation < 0)
at pos 1, attends uniformly over suffix. W_OV maps '(' -> -v,
at pos 1, apply nonlinear thresholding. Neurons fire when != 0
at pos 0, attends ONLY to pos 1. W_OV copies the elevation pos
reads resid[0] projected onto W_U[:,0] - W_U[:,1] = unbalanced
The model works RIGHT-TO-LEFT. Computes elevation over SUFFIXES, not prefixes. It picked this direction randomly - both directions solve the task.
Position 0 is CLASSIFICATION, position 1 is where the ANSWER LIVES. Head 2.0 just moves the signal from pos 1 to pos 0.
Head 2.0's attention pattern is almost degenerate (attends only to pos 1) - a strong hint that its function is 'move info from A to B'.
The OV circuit of head 0.0 is essentially ONE-DIMENSIONAL: v_L approximately -v_R. Head 0.0 projects each token onto ONE 'elevation' direction.
Toy model: bidirectional, classifies at pos 0
BERT-style attention (no causal mask, pad masked at keys), sinusoidal position embeddings, ReLU MLPs, classification at position 0 only.
5-token vocab: [start], [pad], [end], '(', ')'. 2 output classes. 3 layers x 2 heads x d_head=28, d_model = d_mlp = 56.
bidirectional (no causal mask; pad masked at KEYS)
attn_scores = q @ k.T # (batch, n_heads, seq_q, seq_k)
attn = softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1) # pad cols now sum to 0
Bidirectional means query at t sees any key.
But pad tokens are meaningless: mask at KEY dim BEFORE softmax.
If you mask AFTER softmax, other tokens already got some share
of the mass -> you must renormalize. Don't do that.
- Multiple frequencies -> encodes RELATIVE position via a
linear combination of PE[a] and PE[b].
- PE(a + b) is a LINEAR function of PE[a] and PE[b].
Attention can learn to compute relative offsets.
- No new parameters, no train/eval gap for unseen positions.

Two residual pathways per layer: (1) resid_pre -> ln1 -> attention -> add back -> resid_mid. (2) resid_mid -> ln2 -> mlp -> add back -> resid_post.

Goal: find a direction in the residual stream (BEFORE the final LN) such that a high dot product with that direction pushes the classifier toward 'unbalanced'.

From here on I only track:
LN is nonlinear (divide by std) but a linear
fit y = L @ x + c is nearly perfect
∂ Why the LN linear approximation is safe here
LN is y = ((x - mean) / std) * gamma + beta. The nonlinearity is the divide-by-std.
For a fixed input distribution, std is nearly constant across samples.
So over the model's operating distribution, LN acts like y = A @ x + b for some matrix A.
sklearn.LinearRegression finds A directly by fitting LN(x) as a function of x on batch samples.
At seq_pos=0 for THIS model, R^2 > 0.99. The fit is safe to use for direction back-propagation.
For a LARGE LLM this trick can fail: LN is often used to 'clear' the residual stream (one feature grows 100x
larger than everything else, LN divides it out) -> the effective A depends heavily on which feature is active.
In that regime, a global linear fit misses the reality.
The residual just before the final LN is a sum of 10 additive contributions: 1 embed + 6 attn heads + 3 MLPs.
By linearity of dot product, each component's contribution decomposes separately. Histogram per component to find who's responsible.

scanning right-to-left, we ever have more

The MAIN circuit reverse-engineered here handles
When the query is at pos 0, head 2.0's attention puts ~all weight on pos 1. It ignores every other position.
So head 2.0 is essentially: out[0] = W_OV @ resid[1]. The interesting work is UPSTREAM at position 1.

Each MLP neuron has an 'input direction' W_in[:, i] (the KEY) and an 'output direction' W_out[i, :] (the VALUE).
MLP-0 and MLP-1 neurons THRESHOLD the elevation signal. Some fire when open-proportion > 0.5, others when < 0.5.
One MLP neuron: fires when input matches its KEY, writes its VALUE to the residual
MLP(x) = sum over i in [d_mlp] of f( x . W_in[:, i] + b_in[i] ) * W_out[i, :] + b_out
'input direction' = KEY (what activates the neuron). 'output direction' = VALUE (what it writes).

Head 0.0: computing the elevation via uniform-attention + 1D OV
Attention pattern at query pos 1: UNIFORM weight over all key positions >= 1 (ignoring pad).
The OV circuit maps '(' -> -v and ')' -> +v. Cosine similarity v_L vs v_R is approx -1 -> a one-dimensional 'elevation' subspace.
Uniform weight over the whole suffix (positions >= 1)
-> at query pos 1, head averages over the whole rest of the sequence.
Uniform-attention + 1D OV = sum of a per-token feature.
For each bracket char, compute the vector
written when THAT char is the KEY:
So the head projects onto ONE direction v, with
With uniform attention over the suffix:
That's the total elevation in ONE direction.
Extract v_L and v_R from head 0.0's OV circuit
v_L = embedding(model, tokenizer, '(') @ L0.T @ W_OV # vector when key = '('
v_R = embedding(model, tokenizer, ')') @ L0.T @ W_OV # vector when key = ')'
# Head 0.0's OV essentially maps every '(' to -v and every ')' to +v.
The full circuit, working forwards on '(())'
Now I connect all the pieces. Follow one bracket string through the model and see how the elevation signal accumulates.
The four pieces (head 0.0 -> MLPs 0/1 -> head 2.0 -> LN_f + W_U) fit together into the algorithm the model learned.
One forward pass on '(())': how the elevation signal accumulates
Top row: sequence. Colored bars: which positions are active for each lane. Diagonal arrow = head 2.0's pos-1 -> pos-0 copy.
pos 0: attends only to pos 1. W_OV
∂ Worked example: elevation at each position for '(())'
Head 0.0 computes (0.5 - open_proportion) * 2 * v = ((#close - #open) / N) * v at position 1.
For a balanced sequence this is ~ 0. For total-elevation failure it's non-zero.
MLPs threshold that magnitude. Head 2.0 moves the answer to pos 0. W_U reads it.
The main circuit only handles TOTAL-ELEVATION failures via head 0.0's uniform average.
Strings like '())(' pass the count check but are still unbalanced. Some OTHER sub-circuit must detect them.

The bonus explores how far the model can go before
The interp lessons that hold across this notebook and the rest of the ARENA curriculum.
I moved BACKWARDS from logits through softmax -> W_U -> LN -> W_OV to find 'unbalanced directions' at each
residual-stream site. Then FORWARDS from the input to explain how those directions get set.
LayerNorm can be linearised in small models
Fit sklearn.LinearRegression from LN-input to LN-output. R^2 near 1 means the linear approximation works.
This fails in big LLMs where LN is used to 'clear' the residual stream.
Head 2.0's degenerate pattern (attends only to pos 1) told me its role before any weight-level analysis.
Head 0.0's uniform pattern told me it averages over the suffix.
OV dimensionality = what the head is doing
cos(v_L, v_R) approx -1 for head 0.0 means the OV maps two tokens onto opposite ends of ONE direction. The
head projects onto a single feature (elevation).
Head 0.0 AVERAGES a per-token feature into a scalar-in-a-direction. MLPs 0/1 THRESHOLD that scalar
nonlinearly. This aggregate-then-threshold pattern shows up in bigger circuits.
Same technique as for GPT-2 next-token loss. For classification the direction is W_U[:, correct] - W_U[:,
In classification transformers, one position holds the answer. All upstream work is figuring out how to
write the RIGHT thing to that position.
Splitting unbalanced examples by TYPE (total-elevation vs negative) isolated WHICH sub-circuit handles WHICH
failure. Otherwise it looks like a diffuse effect.
The model doesn't know English reading order
The learned algorithm works right-to-left over SUFFIXES. Both directions solve the task. A useful reminder
